Did you choose your last thought, or did it simply arrive? Drawing on Sri Ramakrishna, Holy Mother, Swami Vivekananda, the Bhagavad Gita and the Yoga Sūtras, and on modern science from the stroboscope to Benjamin Libet’s experiment on the timing of decisions, this study shows that free will and Divine Will are not rival powers but one power seen from two places. True freedom is the little “i” coherent with the universal “I”, and surrender is the discipline that brings it about.

Study article: Free Will and Divine Will: Am I the Doer?
By Swami Tadananda
About this study

This study accompanies the Hamilton Satsang of 9 December 2026 and the Satsang Study course on vedanta.nz. It draws on the advanced course The Mind in the Light of Modern and Spiritual Sciences (Module 3, How Experience Is Created). Technical material sits in shaded Going deeper panels, which may be skipped on a first reading. Each part ends with its key idea. Live versions of the figures are in the interactive companion linked in the Introduction.
Introduction: the question we all carry

Free will and Divine Will are not two rival powers. They are one power seen from two places: from inside the little "i", and from the Source from which every impulse flows. This article sets out to show why, step by step, so that a reader with no background in science or scripture can follow the whole argument. On the way we will need to understand how the mind experiences time, because the struggle between "my will" and "Thy will" is, at bottom, an experience in time.
Did you choose your last thought?
Try a small experiment. Sit quietly for a moment and wait for your next thought. When it comes, ask: did I choose it, or did it simply arrive?

Most of us find that thoughts arrive on their own. So do many of our actions. A sudden urge for a snack appears and the hand is already reaching for the biscuit tin. A sharp word leaves the mouth before we have "decided" to say it. Only afterwards does a voice inside say, "I did that."
Yet in the same breath we feel free. We weigh choices, make plans and hold ourselves and others responsible. Both experiences are real. The question is how they fit together.
Why the question matters
This is not only a puzzle for philosophers. How we answer it shapes our peace of mind.
If
I alone am the doer
, every success feeds pride and every failure feeds guilt and anxiety. The whole weight of life rests on one small self.
If
everything is fated
, we may slide into helplessness: why make any effort at all?

The great teachers of the Yoga-Vedanta spiritual tradition offer a third way. We act fully and responsibly, yet without the burden of being the sole doer. Sri Ramakrishna, Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi, Swami Vivekananda and the Bhagavad Gita all point to this freedom, which comes through surrender.
What this article will show
Behind the title lie three questions that every thoughtful person asks sooner or later:
Who really starts my actions?
Do I begin them, or do they arise in me from somewhere deeper?
Is the future already fixed?
If a seer can see what is to come, is everything fated?
Where, then, are my freedom and my responsibility?
And what should I do about it in daily life?
The article answers them in nine parts. Each part opens by naming the question it serves.

Two kinds of "I".

In this article, the little "i" in quotation marks stands for the ego, the I-maker (ahaṁkāra), and the capital "I" for the Self, the Ātman, the witness behind it. Where someone speaks ("I am the doer", "I did it"), the usual capital is kept, as it is in every quotation.
Key idea:
The question "Am I the doer?" can be answered precisely once we see how an experience, and a choice, is formed in the mind.
Part 1: Time is felt in the mind
Serves question 2: Is the future already fixed? Before we can ask who acts in time, we need to ask what time is for the one who experiences it.
We usually think of time as a river flowing at one steady speed for everyone, measured by the clock on the wall. Our own experience tells a different story.
Four everyday observations
Boredom and anxiety.
Waiting for a bus in the rain, or for news from a hospital, a few minutes feel like an hour. We keep checking the clock, and each tick seems to drag.
Absorption.
Watching a gripping film or a close football match, two hours vanish. We do not notice time passing at all, and we are surprised when it ends.
Dreaming.
A few minutes of dream can hold what feels like days, because the dreaming mind keeps its own time, apart from the clock of the waking world.
Deep sleep.
In dreamless sleep there is no time at all. We close our eyes at night and, it seems, open them at once in the morning.

The clock ran at the same rate in all four cases. What changed was the state of the mind. When the mind is restless and set against its situation, time drags. When it is completely absorbed, time disappears from view. When it withdraws altogether, time is not experienced at all.

A first conclusion
Time as we
live
it is not a fixed container outside us. It is an experience in the mind, and it depends on the state of the mind. This is the first building block of our answer.

The spiritual tradition has said this for thousands of years. Swami Vivekananda calls time, space and causation the "walls" within which the mind is bound: "A few steps, and there arises the wall of beginningless and endless time which we cannot surmount" (
Jnana-Yoga
, "Maya and Freedom"). Part 3 will show what happens when the mind goes beyond those walls.

A note for readers who know some physics: Einstein's relativity is about the time measured by clocks, which runs at different rates for different observers. Our subject is time as it is lived in the mind. The two should not be confused, so we leave relativity aside.
Key idea:
The time we live is not a fixed river outside us; it changes with the state of the mind.
Part 2: The stroboscope: reality unchanged, experience changed
Serves question 2. If experience can change while reality stays the same, we must look carefully at what we take to be "really happening", including the feeling "I am doing this".
A mechanic's instrument

A stroboscope is a lamp that flashes very briefly at a frequency you can adjust: ten flashes a second, twelve, and so on. Mechanics use one to tune car engines. Pointed at a part that spins too fast for the eye to follow, it makes the part appear to slow down or stand still, so that its markings can be read.

You may have seen the same effect in films: the wheels of a moving wagon seem to turn slowly, stop, or even turn backwards. The film camera takes pictures at a fixed rate, and it acts like a stroboscope.

Why this matters for us

The stroboscope gives us a precise, everyday model of something the spiritual tradition has long taught. What we experience is not the object alone. It is the meeting of the object with the instrument that perceives it. Change the instrument, and the same reality is experienced as fast, slow, still or even reversed.

In Part 4 we will see that the mind works in a similar way. Attention meets each object with its own rhythm, and the felt sense of time is the difference between them. That is why time drags when we are restless and vanishes when we are absorbed.

The backward motion is worth a passing mention. Some contemplatives describe glimpses of events before they unfold, and the strobe hints at how the felt order of events can, in rare moments, seem to run ahead of their unfolding. We leave it there, because our concern is the will.

Part 3: Those who saw beyond time

Serves question 2. If time depends on the state of the mind, then a mind in a different state may see as present what, for us, has not yet happened. The scriptures and the illumined report exactly this, and it bears directly on who is the doer.

Think of the mind as a dial. Turned one way, it experiences life as a long stream of separate moments. Turned the other way, it holds more and more of time at once, until at the highest setting all of time is present together. The three cases below show the dial at different settings. Read them as data: careful reports of how time is experienced in different states of mind.

Case 1. Narada: half an hour becomes twelve years

Swami Vivekananda tells this story in his London lecture "Maya and Freedom" (22 October 1896). It comes at the end of a series of examples, each ending with the refrain "And this is Maya." Just before it, he says:

With every breath, with every pulsation of the heart with every one of our movements, we think we are free, and the very same moment we are shown that we are not. Bound slaves, nature's bond-slaves, in body, in mind, in all our thoughts, in all our feelings. And this is Maya.
Then he tells the story:

We are all like this in the world. A legend tells how once Nârada said to Krishna, "Lord, show me Maya." A few days passed away, and Krishna asked Narada to make a trip with him towards a desert, and after walking for several miles, Krishna said, "Narada, I am thirsty; can you fetch some water for me?" "I will go at once, sir, and get you water." So Narada went. At a little distance there was a village; he entered the village in search of water and knocked at a door, which was opened by a most beautiful young girl. At the sight of her he immediately forgot that his Master was waiting for water, perhaps dying for the want of it. He forgot everything and began to talk with the girl. All that day he did not return to his Master. The next day, he was again at the house, talking to the girl. That talk ripened into love; he asked the father for the daughter, and they were married and lived there and had children. Thus twelve years passed. His father-in-law died, he inherited his property. He lived, as he seemed to think, a very happy life with his wife and children, his fields and his cattle and so forth. Then came a flood. One night the river rose until it overflowed its banks and flooded the whole village. Houses fell, men and animals were swept away and drowned, and everything was floating in the rush of the stream. Narada had to escape. With one hand he held his wife, and with the other two of his children; another child was on his shoulders, and he was trying to ford this tremendous flood. After a few steps he found the current was too strong, and the child on his shoulders fell and was borne away. A cry of despair came from Narada. In trying to save that child, he lost his grasp upon one of the others, and it also was lost. At last his wife, whom he clasped with all his might, was torn away by the current, and he was thrown on the bank, weeping and wailing in bitter lamentation. Behind him there came a gentle voice, "My child, where is the water? You went to fetch a pitcher of water, and I am waiting for you; you have been gone for quite half an hour." "Half an hour!" Narada exclaimed. Twelve whole years had passed through his mind, and all these scenes had happened in half an hour! And this is Maya.

The same span is "quite half an hour" for Sri Krishna and twelve full years for Narada. Neither is wrong. As Narada's mind falls into Maya, the dial turns down: a short span unrolls into a long stream of moments, each one felt as joy or grief. Notice too that Narada never decided to forget his errand. One thing led to another, and only at the end, in grief, does the question arise: who was living this life?

Case 2. Arjuna: the divine eye, and the war "already" fought
In the eleventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks to see Sri Krishna's universal form. Sri Krishna replies that Arjuna cannot see it with his ordinary eyes, and gives him a divine eye (
divyaṁ dadāmi te cakṣuḥ
, 11.8). The same reality is now seen with a different instrument.

With this eye, Arjuna sees the great warriors of both armies (Bhishma, Drona, Karna and the rest) rushing into the Lord's mouths and perishing (11.26 to 27). The battle has not yet begun on the field, yet he sees its outcome as already present. Sri Krishna explains:
kālo 'smi
, "I am Time" (11.32), and then gives the verse that will be central to this article:
mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvam eva nimitta-mātraṁ bhava savyasācin
"By Me indeed have these already been slain; be thou merely an instrument, O Savyasācin." (Gita 11.33)
When the vision ends, Arjuna's mind returns to its ordinary state (11.51), and the same events once again lie in the future, "not yet happened".
What the story shows.
Here the dial turns up, by grace. The whole war is held in one view. Notice what Sri Krishna does
not
say. He does not tell Arjuna to sit down and let fate unfold. He says "arise" and "be an instrument". The vision removes the claim "I am the doer", not the action. We return to this in Part 8.
Case 3. Sri Ramakrishna: universes rising and falling like waves
In a conversation recorded in
The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

, the Master is speaking with Mahimacharan about the meaning of Om. Mahima explains the three letters a, u and m as creation, preservation and destruction. Sri Ramakrishna gives his own illustration: the sound of a gong, "tom", fading into silence. It is the merging of the Līlā (the play of the relative) in the Nitya (the eternal): the gross, the subtle and the causal merging in the Great Cause, and waking, dream and deep sleep merging in Turīya. The striking of the gong, he says, is like a heavy weight falling into a big ocean. He continues:

"Waves begin to rise: the Relative rises from the Absolute; the causal, subtle, and gross bodies appear out of the Great Cause; from Turiya emerge the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking. These waves arising from the Great Ocean merge again in the Great Ocean. From the Absolute to the Relative, and from the Relative to the Absolute. Therefore I give the illustration of the gong's sound, 'tom'. I have clearly perceived all these things. It has been revealed to me that there exists an Ocean of Consciousness without limit. From It come all things of the relative plane, and in It they merge again. Millions of Brahmandas rise in that Chidakasa and merge in It again."
What the story shows.
This is the top of the dial. The spiritual tradition speaks of three "spaces" (

Chitākāśa
, the inner space of the mind; and
Chidākāśa

brahmāṇḍas

What the three cases share
In every case,
the reality is one and the experience of time differs
with the state of the mind.
The lower the dial, the longer and more fragmented time feels, and the more the "i" seems to be the one living and acting.
The higher the dial, the more is held at once, until events are seen as already complete, and the "i" is seen as an instrument.
The question this raises.

If Arjuna could see the war as already accomplished, is the future already fixed? And if it is, what becomes of choice and effort? We hold this question until Part 8, after we have seen how a choice is actually formed.
Key idea:
The mind is like a dial: the same reality is lived as a long stream of moments or seen as one whole, depending on its setting.

4.3 Time is the beat

Now we can answer the question from Part 1. The course places ordinary, time-bound experience on the side where Δf is not zero, and timeless knowing where Δf is zero. This article takes one further step and makes the link explicit:
the felt passage of time is the beat.
Each beat is one felt "tick" of time.
Large Δf
(the mind out of tune with its object): many beats, each short and thin. Time drags. This is boredom, anxiety, clock-watching. The course describes anxiety as "the beat locked open".
Small Δf
(the mind closely tuned): few beats, each long and full. Time flies. This is the film or the football match.

The object's own unfolding never changes, just as the fan never changed. What changes is how the mind divides it: into many thin moments, or a few full ones, or one undivided whole.

4.5 The second gap: Δφ, the claim "I am the doer"
Δf and Δφ are easy to confuse, so it is worth slowing down here. We take it in four steps: what phase means, what Δφ means in the mind, what the two gaps do together, and what follows for practice.
Step 1: what phase means.

Frequency is how fast a wave turns. Phase is where it stands in its turn at a given moment. Think of two people walking side by side at exactly the same pace. If one steps with the left foot just as the other steps with the right, they are out of step, and walking faster or slower together will never bring them into step. Only a small skip by one of them will. Two clocks show the same thing (Figure 7): both run at the same speed, but one is set five minutes ahead. Adjusting the speed never corrects the setting; the setting must be corrected on its own.

Step 2: Δφ in the mind.

Δf is a difference in rate between attention and its object, and it is felt as time: drag, flow or stillness. Δφ is a standing offset that the I-maker brings to every meeting, whatever the rate. It is the small inner turn that says "this is happening to me", "I am doing this", "this result is mine". Three consequences follow:
Δf can close while Δφ stays.
A person can be completely absorbed in a task, with time vanishing, and still come out of it saying "Look what I achieved." Concentration alone does not remove the claim.
Δφ is felt most in action.
It shows up as pride when things go well, as guilt and anxiety when they go badly, and as the weight of having to hold everything together.
Δφ is the mechanism of sārūpya.
Yoga Sūtra 1.4 (below) speaks of the Seer appearing to take on the form of the vṛtti. The tilt of the I-maker is what makes the vṛtti's actions seem to be the Seer's own.
Step 3: the two gaps together. Experience is a variable.

Put the two gaps together and a simple but far-reaching truth appears. An experience is not a fixed thing that happens to us. It is the result of a meeting in the mind, and it changes as Δf and Δφ change. The same object, met with a different Δf and Δφ, is lived as a different experience: one person's dull evening is another person's absorption. The table sums it up.
Δφ small: the claim released
Δφ large: the claim strong
Δf large: the mind restless
Time drags. The heart is offered, but the mind still wanders.
Time drags. Clarity swells and fades, and every result is "mine".
Δf small: the mind tuned
Time stands still. The object alone shines, full and steady.
Time hardly passes. The experience is steady, but dimmed by the claim.
Only one thing does not change with the dials: the Seer who knows every setting.

How to read Figure 8.

Each panel shows the same object met by the mind for two seconds. The solid line is the experience as lived. Both pictures agree on the essential point. The stricter one adds an insight the spiritual tradition knows well: the subtle ego shows itself most clearly in a concentrated mind.

4.6 The confirmation of the Yoga Sūtras

(taking the same form, identification) and
svarūpa
(one's own form, true nature). The first is bondage; the second is freedom.

Every experience is a meeting of two waves; their difference, Δf, is felt as time, and the I-maker's tilt, Δφ, is felt as "I am the doer".
Part 5: The descent of the Divine Will: the four levels of Vāk
Serves question 1: Who really starts my actions? Part 4 showed how a single experience is formed. Now we follow a single action from its source to its appearance in the world.
5.1 What is will?
We have used the word "will" all along. Before following it on its descent, we should say what it is.
Will is a power, not a thing.

In the spiritual tradition, the power of willing is Icchā Śakti, the Divine Mother's power of will. Swami Vivekananda puts it carefully: "There is something which is not will, but is manifesting itself as will" (
Complete Works
, Vol. 5, "Buddhism and Vedanta"). At its source that power is complete: "The will of God is perfectly fruitful; therefore He is the highest" (Vol. 4, "Our Present Social Problems").
In us, will is a reaction in the mind.

"When the mind perceives, then, as the reaction, it wills. The will is in the mind" (letter to E. T. Sturdy, Vol. 8). So every vṛtti carries a little will. I will eat, I will sleep, I will work, I will play: each has a content (what), a direction (the push towards doing it) and a claim (the "i"). The push is the will. Swamiji calls it "the 'still small voice', the real Ruler who says 'do' and 'do not'" (
Inspired Talks

Notice the order. For the Divine Mother, will comes first: Icchā, then Jñāna, then Kriyā. For the individual mind, knowledge comes first and will follows as its reaction. Both are true. Her will is prior, at Paśyantī; our "I will" is its reflection in the mind, at Madhyamā, after the impulse has taken the form of knowledge. That is exactly where Libet's volunteers felt their urge (Part 6).
Many little wills, one mighty will.

Most of the time our little wills pull in different directions: I want to meditate, I want to sleep, I want to check my phone. They largely cancel each other, and we call the result a weak will. When they line up, they add. Waves behave in just this way: a hundred waves out of step add up to only about ten times the strength of one, while a hundred in step add up to a hundred times. Figure 9 shows the idea. Swamiji explains how a will grows strong. Energy spent on selfish ends is frittered away, but held back it becomes power: "This self-control will tend to produce a mighty will, a character which makes a Christ or a Buddha." And it is built by work over time: "this will is caused by character, and character is manufactured by Karma. As is Karma, so is the manifestation of the will" (
Karma-Yoga
, "Karma in its Effect on Character").

A strong will is still bound.

Strength is not freedom. "The will is not free, it is a phenomenon bound by cause and effect, but there is something behind the will which is free" (Vol. 5, "Sayings and Utterances"). And again: "That which seems to be the will is the Atman behind, it is really free" (

Will has two directions.
"The ignorant will leads to bondage, the knowing will can free us. The will can be made strong in thousands of ways; every way is a kind of Yoga" (
Inspired Talks

Education is the training of the will.

Swamiji's definition of education is really a definition of the work of this whole study: "The training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful is called education" (Vol. 4, "Our Present Social Problems"). Every practice in Part 9 is such a training.

Will in Swami Vivekananda's words.

He calls will "a compound, a mixture of the internal and the external": without senses and an outside world there would be no will (Vol. 5, "Buddhism and Vedanta"). He speaks of its power because of its source: "The will is stronger than anything else. Everything must go down before the will, for that comes from God and God Himself; a pure and a strong will is omnipotent" (Vol. 3, "My Plan of Campaign"). And of will through evolution: "You have developed from the lowest amoeba. Continue to exercise your will and it will take you higher still", adding that when we doubt its power, "you are thinking only of your little self" (Vol. 2, "Practical Vedanta", Part IV).
5.2 A choice is also a vṛtti

Part 4 dealt with perception: a sound, a face, a situation. But a wish, an intention and a decision are also waves in the mind. "I will speak now", "I will reach for the cup", "I will forgive him": each rises in citta, shaped by saṁskāras, by the state of the body and prāṇa, and by the whole situation, just like any other vṛtti. And like any other vṛtti, it is claimed by Δφ: "I decided."

This is the step that connects time to will. If a choice is a vṛtti, it does not appear from nowhere at the moment we notice it. It has a history. It rises from somewhere subtler and takes form on its way to action. So the question "Who starts my actions?" becomes two questions: where does this wave come from, and at what point does the "i" step in?
5.3 The four levels of the Word

The spiritual tradition of Kashmir Shaivism gives a precise map of this descent. It speaks of the creative power of the Divine Mother as Vāk, the Word, and of Her power of will as Icchā Śakti. Every impulse, from the creation of a universe to the movement of a hand, flows from the Supreme Source through four levels:
Parā Vāk, the Supreme.
The Source itself, beyond time and beyond the equation of Part 4. Here the will of the Divine Mother is pure potential, undivided from Herself.
Paśyantī, "the one who sees": Icchā, will.

The first stirring. The impulse is whole and wordless, seen all at once rather than unfolded in sequence. This is the widest band, nearest the Source, where Δf is close to zero. There is no "i" here yet, only will.
Madhyamā, "the middle": Jñāna, knowledge.

The impulse takes shape as an idea, an intention, a thought in the space of the mind: the knowledge space. The band is narrower, and the whole begins to unfold as a sequence of ideas. Here the vṛtti becomes something I can notice, and here the I-maker's tilt, Δφ, attaches: "I want", "I have decided".
Vaikharī, "the outward": Kriyā, action.
The impulse appears as spoken words and bodily action in space and time. This is the narrowest band, where Δf is widest and everything happens one moment after another.

Below the Supreme, then, are three bandwidths of decreasing frequency, through which one impulse flows until it becomes a thought in the knowledge space and then an act in the world. In the language of our course, the descent runs from the spectral domain, where the whole is present at once, into the temporal domain, where it unfolds moment by moment.

As Figure 10 shows, the same impulse narrows as it descends. The "i" appears only at Madhyamā, where the impulse first takes a form it can recognise and claim.
5.4 Watching the descent in yourself: speaking a sentence

You can watch this descent in your own experience. Before you say something important, there is a moment when you know what you mean, whole, before a single word has formed. That has the flavour of Paśyantī. Then the meaning takes shape as words in the mind, which you can hear inwardly and revise: Madhyamā. Then the words leave the mouth one syllable at a time: Vaikharī. The meaning was complete at the start. Speaking only unrolls it in time.

Now notice where the "i" appears. In the first moment there is only meaning. The sense "I am going to say this" arrives with the inner words. By the time the sentence is spoken, the "i" is sure it was the author from the beginning.
5.5 What the descent shows
The impulse does not begin with the "i".
It begins at the Source, as the Divine Mother's will, and passes through will and knowledge before it becomes action.
The "i" steps in midway, at Madhyamā,
and claims what was already moving. That claim is Δφ.
"My free will" and "Divine Will" are one movement seen from two places.
Seen from inside, after the claim, it feels like my free will. Seen from its Source, it is the Divine Will.

Arjuna's vision (Part 3) is this descent seen at the cosmic scale, from the side of the Source: the whole war present at once. In Part 6 we will see the same descent caught, at the finest scale, in a neuroscience laboratory.
This is a contemplative map, drawn from spiritual experience, not a scientific finding. Its value is that it makes sense both of what science observes and of what the illumined report.
Key idea:
Every action descends from the Divine Source through will, knowledge and deed; the "i" appears midway, at Madhyamā, and claims as its own what was already flowing.
Part 6: Libet's experiment: the late arrival of the "i"
Serves question 1. Modern science has tried to catch the moment of decision in the act. What it found matches the descent of Part 5 with remarkable precision.
6.1 The experiment

In 1983 the American neuroscientist Benjamin Libet and his colleagues carried out one of the most discussed experiments in the science of the mind. Volunteers sat in front of a fast-moving dot on a clock face. Whenever they felt like it, they flexed their wrist. They then reported where the dot had been at the moment they first felt the urge to move.

Libet's experiment: the set-up
All the while, electrodes on the scalp recorded a slow build-up of electrical activity in the brain, known as the
readiness potential
. (It had first been described by Kornhuber and Deecke in 1965.)
When the three timings were lined up, the result surprised everyone:
The brain's readiness potential began about
0.55 seconds
before the movement.
The volunteers' awareness of the urge ("now I want to move") came only about
0.2 seconds
before the movement.
So the brain had begun preparing about
a third of a second before
the person was aware of deciding.

The readiness potential rises from about 0.55 seconds before the movement; the urge is felt only about 0.2 seconds before it, leaving a brief "veto" window. When the act is completed, the potential peaks at the movement and then falls back to baseline. In a later study (1985), Libet reported that when people vetoed a planned act after feeling the urge, the build-up flattened and fell away before the movement time.

6.2 What scientists have made of it
The experiment has been debated for forty years. Four main readings stand out, and it is important to present them fairly.
"The brain decides, and consciousness only reports."

On this view the decision is made unconsciously, and the feeling "I chose" is a story told afterwards. The psychologist Daniel Wegner called it "the illusion of conscious will". Later brain-scanning studies seemed to support it, predicting simple left-or-right choices a few seconds early, though only somewhat better than chance.
"Free won't."

Libet himself pointed out that the 0.2 seconds between the urge and the movement leaves a short window in which the action can still be stopped. We may not start our impulses, he suggested, but we can veto them.
"No decision until the threshold."

In 2012, Aaron Schurger and colleagues proposed that the readiness potential is not a hidden decision at all. The brain's activity rises and falls all the time, like background noise; the readiness potential may simply be those rises, caught on their way to a tipping point. On this reading the real "decision" happens only when the threshold is crossed, close to the moment of awareness.
Questions of method.
Reporting "when I felt the urge" by watching a clock is itself unreliable, and flexing a wrist at a random moment is very different from a real choice made for a reason.
The fair summary.
Science has not settled whether we have free will. But in every reading, a great deal of what leads to an action happens before the "i" knows of it, and then the "i" claims it.
6.3 The light of Yoga-Vedanta
Now read the same results with the framework of Part 4.
The meeting forms first.

A vṛtti, an urge to move, is already forming in the field of the mind, from saṁskāras, the state of the body and the whole situation, before its beat reaches clear awareness. The readiness potential is the outer trace of this forming.
Then the claim.
Only afterwards does ahaṁkāra's tilt, Δφ, attach itself to the vṛtti: "
I
decided to move." In the language of Part 5, this is the impulse reaching Madhyamā, where it first takes a form the "i" can recognise and claim. This is the late "i" that Libet's clock caught.
It does not depend on which scientific reading wins.

If the brain "decides first" (reading 1), the vṛtti forms before the I-maker claims it. If the decision happens at the threshold (reading 3), the background fluctuations are the vast field of impressions and conditions, and the threshold is where they come together into one act. Either way, the doer the ego claims to be arrives late.
The veto has its place.
The "free won't" of reading 2 matches the yogic pause, the moment of discrimination (
viveka

) in which a rising impulse can be seen and not followed. This is real and valuable. But the veto is not the "i" overruling the Source. It is a second impulse, discrimination, which also descends from the Source and meets the first at Madhyamā, carried by the saṁskāras of practice. The "i" then claims this too: "I chose not to." It is the work of a well-tuned instrument, not proof of an independent doer.
Can the ego veto what has begun at a subtler level?

Not on its own. Science finds the veto real but limited: in a later study, people could still cancel a movement after the readiness potential had begun, but only up to a point of no return, about 0.2 seconds before the muscles moved (Schultze-Kraft and colleagues, 2016). Science does not say who or what does the vetoing; a veto has its own preparation in the brain, just as the movement does. In the light of Vāk, nothing that has begun at a subtler level is cancelled from below. Two currents descend, the impulse and the counter-impulse of discrimination, and the stronger prevails. The Gita states the limit of the ego's own veto plainly (18.59 to 60). If, from egoism, Arjuna resolves "I will not fight", that resolve is vain: his own nature will compel him, and bound by his own karma he will do even what, in delusion, he does not wish to do. A veto made from ego, against one's nature, does not hold. A veto rooted in discrimination, grown through practice, does, because it too comes from deeper than the "i".
“Your very bones will do it.”

Swami Vivekananda’s own life shows the same truth. Towards the end of Sri Ramakrishna’s life, at the Cossipore garden house, the Master wrote on a piece of paper, “Naren will teach people.” Narendra, as he then was, refused. He later recalled to M.: “But I said to him, ‘I won’t do any such thing.’ Thereupon he said, ‘Your very bones will do it.’” (The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, “After the Passing Away”). The resolve “I will not” came from the little “i”; his nature, shaped by the Divine Will, carried him past it. As Swami Vivekananda he went on to carry the message of Vedanta across the world.
Swami Vivekananda said it in London in 1896, almost a century before Libet's clock:
"With every breath, with every pulsation of the heart with every one of our movements, we think we are free, and the very same moment we are shown that we are not." (
Jnana-Yoga
, "Maya and Freedom")

Read this way, the readiness potential is the outer trace of an impulse already descending through Paśyantī, before it has any form the "i" can notice. The felt urge, about 0.2 seconds before the movement, marks its arrival at Madhyamā: the impulse now has a form, the "i" recognises it, and says "I want to move". The movement itself is Vaikharī. The veto belongs to Madhyamā too: once the impulse has a form the mind can see, a second impulse, discrimination, can meet it there and decline to carry it out.

So the half-second Libet measured is a tiny glimpse, at the finest scale, of the same descent that Arjuna saw on a cosmic scale: action rising from the Divine Source through will, knowledge and deed, with the "i" arriving midway to say "I did it".
Key idea:
Libet's experiment shows the action forming before the "i" knows of it; the descent of Vāk explains why: the impulse rises from the Source, and the "i" claims it only at Madhyamā.
Part 7: Two dials: Δf and Δφ

Serves question 3: Where are my freedom and my responsibility? We now have everything we need to answer the question in the title. Part 4 gave us two gaps. Here they become two dials, and freedom depends on both.
7.1 The first dial, Δf: my will and Her will

Apply the framework of Part 4 to the question of will itself. In Part 4 the "object" was whatever attention meets: a sound, a face, a task. Here the object is the whole of what is actually unfolding in our life.
The individual will
is the attention-wave of the person, with its own rhythm, f
m
: my wishes, plans, fears and preferences, coloured by saṁskāra.
The Divine Will
is the one reality that is actually unfolding, with its own rhythm, f
s

: what Sri Krishna showed Arjuna as "already" accomplished, and what the spiritual tradition calls the will of the Divine Mother, Parāśakti, unfolding through Her powers of will, knowledge and action.

When the two are far apart, Δf is large. Then we feel the familiar struggle: "my will" against "fate" or "God's will". Life feels like friction, effort and pressure. Time drags and every moment is a battle. When they come closer, the beat slows; life begins to flow. When they are one, Δf = 0: there is no beat left to feel as two wills at all.

So the conflict between free will and Divine Will is not a fact about reality. It is the beat produced by the gap between them. It is real as an experience, just as the fan's apparent motion was real to the eye, but it is not the deepest truth.

7.2 The second dial, Δφ: who is the doer?
The second gap, Δφ, the tilt of the I-maker, explains the feeling "I did it". The Bhagavad Gita states it directly:
prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ / ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā kartāham iti manyate
"The Gunas of Prakriti perform all action. With the understanding deluded by egoism, man thinks, 'I am the doer.'" (Gita 3.27, tr. Swami Swarupananda)
And it describes where the true Doer dwells:
"The Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings, by His illusive power, to revolve, as if mounted on a machine." (Gita 18.61)
Sri Ramakrishna, asked by Vaidyanath whether we are really free to do whatever we like, answered:

"Everything depends on the will of God. ... As long as a man has not realized God, he thinks he is free. It is God Himself who keeps this error in man. Otherwise sin would have multiplied. Man would not have been afraid of sin, and there would have been no punishment for it."
And of the one who has realised God:

"He feels: 'I am the machine, and Thou, O Lord, art the Operator. I am the house and Thou art the Indweller. I am the chariot and Thou art the Driver. I move as Thou movest me; I speak as Thou makest me speak.'"
To Keshab Chandra Sen he said: "Not even a leaf moves except by the will of God."

Notice the remarkable phrase: "It is God Himself who keeps this error in man." The feeling of being a free, independent doer is not a mistake to be ashamed of. At our present setting of the dial, it is necessary. It keeps us responsible and careful until we see more truly. This is Δφ seen with compassion.
7.3 Swami Vivekananda: the will is bound, the Self is free
Swami Vivekananda takes the argument to its root. In
Karma-Yoga
("Freedom") he says that "there cannot be any such thing as free will; the very words are a contradiction," because will, like everything we know, is moulded by time, space and causation. In
Jnana-Yoga

("The Real and the Apparent Man") he puts it in five words: "Free will is a misnomer. Will can never be free." And in "The Free Soul" (New York, 1896): "Will is a portion of that being, caught in the network of Maya, and therefore 'free will' is a misnomer."
But he does not stop at bondage. In his class notes he adds the decisive point:
"The will can never be free, because it is the slave of cause and effect. But the 'I' behind the will is free; and this is the Self." (
Complete Works
, Vol. 6)
This is exactly the distinction of Part 4. The will belongs to the meeting, to the world of Δf and time. Freedom belongs to the Seer,
svarūpa
, which is beyond the equation altogether. We were looking for freedom in the wrong place. It is not in the late "i" that claims the action, but in the Self that witnesses it.
7.4 Two dials, four ways of living
Because the two dials are separate, there are four broad ways of living. Most of us move between them several times in a single day.

imageData.altText: Figure 14. Two dials, four ways of living (schematic)

textData.text: Figure 14.
Two dials, four ways of living (schematic)
Restless and self-centred.
The mind is out of tune with what is happening, and the "i" holds every result. Life feels like struggle and friction; time drags; every outcome is mine to carry.
Focused but self-centred.
Many capable, high-achieving people live here. The work is excellent, and time flies while doing it, yet the claim remains: every success inflates, every failure wounds.
Devoted but scattered.
The heart has offered itself, but the mind is not yet steady enough to hold the offering. Sincerity is there; steadiness is still to come.
Focused and surrendered.
This is the instrument: Arjuna after the vision, the actor who never forgets the role is a role. Full effort, full attention, and no claim. In Sri Ramakrishna's words, "I move as Thou movest me."
Why concentration alone does not free us.

Meditation and concentration close Δf, and they bring real gifts: clarity, calm and a widening of the present moment. But a sharp mind can still be a proud mind, and the spiritual tradition warns that powers gained through concentration can strengthen the ego rather than dissolve it. Freedom needs the second dial too: the claim must be offered. The two dials also help each other. A mind that has let go of the claim has less to defend, so it settles more easily; and a settled mind sees more clearly that the claim was never true.
7.5 The answer: the little "i" coherent with the universal "I"
We can now answer the question "Am I the doer?"
Free will, as an independent power of the little "i", is the late arrival Libet's clock caught
: real as an experience, but not the source of action.
The Divine Will is not a foreign power imposed on us.
It is the one reality unfolding, of which our own being is a part.
True freedom is not independence from the Divine Will but coherence with it.
In physics, two waves are
coherent

when they keep a fixed relationship in time, which requires the same frequency (Δf = 0). Coherence alone is not enough: two coherent waves held half a cycle apart cancel each other out. When they are both coherent and in phase (Δφ = 0), they add fully. So it is with the little "i" and the universal "I". When the little "i" moves at the same rhythm as the universal "I" and has given up its tilt, the two add fully: in the course's words, the object alone shining, at double fullness. "Thy will be done" is not defeat. It is coherence.
Key idea:
Free will and Divine Will meet on two dials: Δf, closed by practice, and Δφ, released by surrender; freedom is the little "i" coherent with the universal "I", not independent of It.
Part 8: But am I still responsible?

Serves questions 2 and 3. If the Divine Mother is the Doer, and the seer sees the war as already won, a newcomer will rightly ask: is everything fated? Why make any effort? Am I still responsible for what I do?
8.1 Is everything fated?
Arjuna saw the war as already accomplished. Yet in the same verse Sri Krishna told him: "Therefore arise" (Gita 11.33). The vision did not make the action unnecessary. It changed who was acting.

The key is the difference between two vantage points. From an aeroplane, the whole of a winding mountain road can be seen at once: every bend, and where it ends. For the driver on that road, every bend must still be steered, one after another, with full attention. The view from above does not take the steering wheel out of the driver's hands. In the same way, what is "already complete" to a mind at the top of the dial (Part 3) is, for us at our setting, a road still to be driven. For one who lives in time, choice and effort are real and necessary.

Fatalism makes a hidden mistake. It keeps the claim, Δφ, and simply turns it towards doing nothing: "Since it is all decided, I need not bother." That is still the little "i" deciding. Surrender is the opposite: full effort, with the claim given up.
8.2 Freedom within limits

A teaching of Sri Ramakrishna, often retold in the Ramakrishna Order, puts this in a homely image. A cow is tied by a rope to a post. Within the length of its rope it is free: it can move about and graze, and if it is to eat, it must make the effort. But it cannot go beyond the rope. When the grass within reach is used up, the cowherd moves the post to fresh pasture.

In the terms of this article, the post and the length of the rope are set by our past karma: the saṁskāras that shape every vṛtti (Part 4). Within that range, effort is ours to make, and it matters. The moving of the post is grace.

Recall too Sri Ramakrishna's words in Part 7: "It is God Himself who keeps this error in man. Otherwise sin would have multiplied." The sense of being a free doer is given to us for a reason. As long as we feel that we are the doer, we must also feel responsible. The teaching does not cancel responsibility. Responsibility is the form the teaching takes at our present setting of the dial.
8.3 Effort, karma and grace
Karma is the shape of the field.
The saṁskāras, h(t) in the equation of Part 4, colour every new impulse. They decide where the post stands.
Effort is what we do within the field.
It is how both dials are turned: practice closes Δf, and offering releases Δφ. Effort also lays down new saṁskāras, so today's effort becomes tomorrow's field.
Grace is the Divine Mother's movement towards us.
It is the moving of the post, the breeze that is always blowing (Part 9). Effort does not compel grace, but it prepares the mind to receive it.
Effort and grace are not rivals. Effort is how the claim is gradually given up; grace is what is found when it is.
8.4 Two levels, not rivals

Sri Ramakrishna gives the balance in practical terms: do your duties in the world as if you were the doer, but know all the time that God alone is the Doer and you are the instrument. Both levels are true, each in its place.
The two levels can be set side by side. Read across each row: the same life, seen from the person and seen from the Self.
Aspect
At the level of the person (Δf ≠ 0)
At the level of the Self (beyond the equation)
Who acts
We choose carefully and take responsibility for our actions
The Divine Mother is the Doer; we are Her instruments
Effort and result
We make effort, and use discrimination to pause and "veto" an impulse
The witness is untouched by success and failure
Time
Time flows, and we plan for the future
All is present; the outcome is already held
How we live it
Act fully, as if we were the doer
Know all the while that God alone is the Doer
Think of a fine actor. He plays his role with complete commitment, weeping and laughing on stage, yet he never forgets that he is not the character. Both levels are true at once.
Key idea:
The future may be complete in the sight of the Divine, but for us it is a road still to be driven: effort and responsibility are real, and they are the very means by which the claim is given up.
Part 9: Surrender: the discipline that turns both dials
Serves question 3. If freedom is coherence with the Divine Will, then the practical question is how to turn the two dials. The great teachers give one answer: surrender.
9.1 Holy Mother's story of the fish
In
The Gospel of Holy Mother

, recorded by Swami Ishanananda, Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi is speaking about the power of the Divine Mother's Māyā. No amount of japa or work, she says, will open the way unless Mahāmāyā Herself opens it. And so she urges: "Surrender, surrender. Then alone will She take compassion on you and leave your path open."

She then tells an incident from Sri Ramakrishna's life at Kamarpukur. During heavy monsoon rains he was walking along the main road, wading through flooded fields, where villagers were beating the stranded fish with sticks. One fish kept circling his feet. Sri Ramakrishna told them not to kill it, for it "is going round my feet, surrendering itself to me", and he set it free in the pond. Then he remarked: "Ah, if anyone could surrender in this manner, then alone can he find protection."

The other fish struggled and were caught. The one that stopped struggling and turned to the Master's feet was saved. In the language of this article, it gave up the claim to save itself (Δφ released), and in that same act it stopped fighting the current (Δf closing). Both dials turned together.
9.2 Surrender is not giving up
Surrender is often misunderstood as passivity or defeat. It is neither.
It is
not giving up effort
. Arjuna fought; Holy Mother worked tirelessly all her life.
It is
giving up the claim
. What is surrendered is Δφ, the I-maker's tilt: "I alone am doing this, and the result must be mine."
It is
tuning, not stopping
. Surrender works first on Δφ. As the claim is released, resistance falls away; a mind with nothing to defend grows steady, and Δf begins to close as well. Action then flows rather than grinds.
The Gita's last great teaching gathers this up:
"Abandoning all DHARMAS, (of the body, mind, and intellect), take refuge in Me alone; I will liberate thee from all sins; grieve not." (Gita 18.66)
Mā śucaḥ
: grieve not. Freedom from grief and guilt is the fruit of surrender, because the burden of being the sole doer has been laid down.
Swami Brahmananda, the spiritual son of Sri Ramakrishna, gives the same teaching as an image:
"The breeze of grace is always blowing; unfurl your sails." (
The Eternal Companion
We do not create the wind. Our part is to unfurl the sails: to prepare the mind so that it can receive what is always being given.
9.3 Practices for turning the two dials

Surrender is a discipline, practised in small moments. Here are some practices, each marked with the dial it mainly turns: Δφ (releasing the claim), Δf (tuning the mind), or both. Choose one or two to begin with.
Pause in the gap (Δφ).
Before you speak or react, take one breath. This is Libet's "veto" window made conscious: the moment at Madhyamā when an impulse has taken form but not yet become action. It gives discrimination (
viveka
) a moment to act. The pause cannot be commanded by the ego. It is cultivated, little by little, until it rises by itself.
Offer before you begin (Δφ).

Before a task, offer it silently to the Divine Mother. Swami Brahmananda taught a threefold prayer for work: before beginning, pray for strength to do it unselfishly; during it, for strength to do it well; and when it is done, offer the result to God.
Work as an instrument (Δφ).
Give your full effort, and leave the result to Her. When praise or blame comes, notice who claims it.
Accept what comes (both).
When things do not go as planned, try saying inwardly: "This is Your will for today." Notice how the claim loosens and the beat of resistance softens.
Steady the rhythm (Δf).
Slow breathing, regular routines and japa steady the mind's rhythm (f
m
), so that Δf is no longer erratic. The course notes that breath slowed to about six breaths a minute gives the system a stable reference.
Evening review (both).
Before sleep, look back over the day: where did I fight the current, and where did I flow? Who was the doer today, the I-maker or the instrument?
Meditation (Δf).

Daily dhāraṇā and dhyāna are the direct training of saṁyama, the practice that reduces the beat. As the mind settles, the window of the present widens, and moments of timeless stillness begin to appear.
9.4 Design your own practice
Each life is different: a parent at home, a nurse on shift, a student before exams, a retiree. Take a few minutes to design one practice for your own week.
Where
in my week does the beat run hardest: a meeting, the commute, a difficult conversation?
What
will I do there: a breath, an offering, a silent phrase?
How
will I remember: a note on the phone, a picture on the desk, the moment of washing my hands?
Bring your practice and your experience of it to the next satsang, or share it in the Satsang Study group.
Key idea:
Surrender is not giving up effort but giving up the claim; it releases Δφ, and as the claim falls away the mind grows steady and Δf closes too.
Conclusion: from the beat to the stillness
We began with three questions. We can now answer them.
Who really starts my actions?

Not the little "i". Every action is a vṛtti that descends from the Divine Source through will (Paśyantī), knowledge (Madhyamā) and deed (Vaikharī). The "i" steps in midway and claims it, and Libet's clock caught it arriving late. The true Doer is the Divine Mother, acting through us as Her instruments.
Is the future already fixed?

To a mind at the top of the dial, all is present at once: Arjuna saw the war already accomplished, and Sri Ramakrishna saw universes rising and falling like waves. But time as we live it is an experience in the mind, felt through Δf, and for us the road must still be driven. Seeing the whole from above does not remove the need to steer.
Where, then, are my freedom and my responsibility?

Freedom is not in the will, which is bound, but in the Self behind the will, which is ever free. In daily life we move towards it by turning two dials: tuning the mind through practice, so that Δf closes, and releasing the claim through surrender, so that Δφ falls away. Until the claim is gone, responsibility remains ours, and effort is how we give the claim up. When both dials are turned, the little "i" becomes coherent with the universal "I".

Sri Ramakrishna's image of the gong gathers it all. When the gong is struck, "tom", the sound rings out and then fades, merging into silence, as the gross, the subtle and the causal merge in the Great Cause. Our lives, our choices and our struggles are the ringing. The Divine Will is the silence from which the sound arose and into which it returns. To surrender is to let the ringing settle, and to discover that the silence was never absent.
